v: Long before the CTrain, Calgary had streetcars. Then it got rid of them.
In April, nineteen oh seven, Calgary voters approved a street railway owned by the city itself.
On July fifth, nineteen oh nine, the first cars rolled, just in time for the fair, on a line out to the exhibition grounds.
Twelve streetcars, on twenty-five point seven kilometres of track, for a community of thirty thousand people.
The network grew fast, until the boom ended in nineteen thirteen.
And the tracks shaped the city. Streetcar suburbs like South Calgary grew along the lines. A streetcar loop there helped give Marda Loop its name.
Out west, a developer offered the city two islands for a park, if it ran streetcars over his bridge. The city agreed. Those islands became Bowness Park.
But in nineteen forty-six, the system was renamed the Calgary Transit System, and the city chose trolley coaches and gas buses instead.
Route by route, the streetcars were phased out. The last one ran in nineteen fifty.
For more than thirty years, Calgary's transit ran without rails.
Then, in nineteen seventy-eight, construction began on the CTrain. On May twenty-fifth, nineteen eighty-one, it opened: ten point nine kilometres, from Anderson Road to Seventh Avenue Southwest.
Four retired streetcar motor-conductors rode that first run.
One of them, Percy Langley, told the Calgary Herald: those streetcars were a damned nuisance. These are a lot better.
And in a possible nod to the old streetcars, whose routes once had colours, that first line was briefly called the Blue Line.
The very last streetcar? It was restored, and it sits at Heritage Park.
The first cars rolled in nineteen oh nine. By nineteen fifty, they were gone.
When the CTrain opened in nineteen eighty-one, four retired streetcar motor-conductors rode the first run.
